measures.t: Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 concerns state and local taxes.
measures.q:
Initiative Measure No. IP26-645 concerns state and local taxes.
This measure would repeal a 9.9% tax on annual individual income over $1,000,000; prohibit taxes measured by individual income and taxes on individual income or the receipt of individual income; and define “income.”
This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare).
Should this measure be enacted into law?
measures.s: This measure would repeal a 9.9% tax on annual individual income over $1,000,000; prohibit state and local governments from imposing taxes on individual income or the receipt of individual income and taxes measured by an individual’s income; and define income as “any gain or benefit measured in money derived from an individual’s capital, labor, property, or other source.” It would also define “individual” as a natural person for purposes of excise taxes.
measures.sb: The Attorney General's Office: the ballot measure summary in its ballot title letter of May 4, 2026. It is not printed on the ballot.
measures.f: If approved by voters, Initiative 645 will result in an estimated loss to state revenue of $11.4 billion over state fiscal years 2027-2031. This would reduce funding to the state general fund to support core government services, particularly public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare). The Legislature expressed an intent to use the additional revenue created by Engrossed Substitute Senate Bill 6346 (2026) (ESSB 6346) towards providing free school meals, transferring funds for childcare and early learning, and transferring funds to local governments to mitigate sales tax loss.
measures.fb: The Office of Financial Management: the summary of its fiscal impact statement, printed in the state voters' pamphlet.
measures.r: To pass, the measure needs more YES votes than NO votes. It also fails if the votes cast on it are fewer than one third of all the votes cast in the election. (Washington Constitution, article II, section 1(d); Revised Code of Washington 29A.60.260)
measures.h: A citizens' initiative to the people, filed as IP26-645, certified to the November 3, 2026 ballot by the Secretary of State. It would repeal chapter 238, Laws of 2026 (the tax on individual income over $1,000,000 that the Legislature passed that year).
measures.nt: The ballot prints the statement of subject and the concise description that make up the Attorney General's ballot title (letter of May 4, 2026), then a sentence that is not in that letter: "This measure would decrease funding for public K-12 education, higher education (including universities and community colleges), and human services (primarily healthcare)." That sentence is the public investment impact disclosure the Attorney General supplied on July 23, 2026. State law requires such a disclosure for a measure that would reduce state revenue and places it after the concise description and before the question, but says it is not part of the ballot title. The question shown follows the Attorney General's letter of July 23, which sets out how the ballot displays both, and matches the printed voters' pamphlet.

measures.t: Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in public school.
measures.q:
Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 concerns parental rights relating to their children in public school.
This measure would repeal amendments to a statute listing certain rights of parents and guardians of public-school children and re-enact the law as it was originally enacted by Initiative to the Legislature 2081.
Should this measure be enacted into law?
measures.s: This measure would re-enact RCW 28A.605.005 as it was originally enacted in Initiative to the Legislature 2081. The re-enacted law would list certain rights of parents and guardians of public-school children, including rights to review materials and student records, receive certain notifications and opt students out of certain activities. It would repeal amendments to the statute, which modified school obligations and access to certain student records and added certain parental rights.

measures.t: Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools.
measures.q:
Initiative Measure No. IL26-638 concerns participation in athletics at K-12 schools.
This measure would prohibit students it defines as “biologically male” from competing in certain school athletic activities intended for female students only. It would require verification of biological sex by students’ healthcare providers.
Should this measure be enacted into law?
measures.s: This measure would require policies prohibiting students it defines as “biologically male” from competing with or against female students in certain interschool athletic activities that are intended for female students only. Students who choose to participate in such activities must provide a statement from the student’s healthcare provider verifying the student’s biological sex, based on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels. These requirements would apply to individual or team athletic competitions.

methods: lists

Who is running comes only from the Washington Secretary of State’s own lists of candidates for the November 3 general election, and the official primary results; each file is named below, with where it was read. The U.S. Senate and House races are on the Congress pages. County and local contests are read from the lists named below too: which local offices are on this ballot, what was read and what is not here yet are set out under County by county, in the words of the notes kept with the lists.
lists

What is read from the lists. The office and the district or place it belongs to, the candidate’s name, the party, the ballot order where the list gives one, the official primary vote counts where they are loaded, and the campaign website where a candidate listed one. Addresses, phone numbers and e-mail in the lists are never read, kept or shown.
lists

Parties. Offices elected on party lines show the party each candidate filed under, written out. Judges are on the nonpartisan ballot; the page says so instead of a party. Among the county and local contests here, cities and other districts are nonpartisan; county offices are some of each. Each contest’s own page says which, from the list it was read from.
lists
Order. Candidates appear in the ballot order the list gives, or by surname where it gives none. Never by money, polls or party.
places

Places. A county or local contest is filed under every county it reaches. The names of cities, towns and districts come from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Washington Secretary of State, each named among these sources.
holders

Who holds a seat today (the Legislature and the statewide offices the roster carries) comes from the Open States roster the record side of this site uses. A candidate matched to a sitting legislator by district and name, one fit only, links to their record page, and their birth date, terms and portrait come from that roster before anything else.
maps

The map and “use my location”. The lines on the map of “your ballot” come from the Washington Secretary of State, the WaTech (State of Washington), the King County GIS, the Clark County GIS, Spokane County, the Snohomish County GIS, the Kittitas County GIS, Clallam County, the Pierce County Auditor, the U.S. Census Bureau and the Washington State Legislature: precincts, the districts put together from whole precincts, and the larger districts’ own lines; each source’s own notice is shown with the map. The Legislature’s page draws the Census Bureau’s cartographic boundary files. Your location is used on your own device to find your precinct and is never sent anywhere. The exact spot is not kept: what stays on the device until you tap “Forget” is your precinct with its districts and a rounded copy of the spot (about half a mile). A typed address goes from your device straight to the U.S. Census Bureau’s address finder, only when you press Look up; only the spot it finds comes back, used the same way, and this site never sees or keeps the address. Street pictures are off until you switch them on; then they come from OpenStreetMap’s servers, which see which map squares are asked for. Your county’s sample ballot is the authority on your ballot.
page
Nobody is scored or graded. The cards show the record; the judging is yours.
people

Who the candidates are. For the Legislature, judges, county offices, mayors and city councils a card may show a photo, an age, the public offices a candidate has held, the government’s own page about an officeholder, the campaign’s website and the headings of its issues page. Official records come first; the rest was found on the open web by one reader and confirmed against the page that states it by a second, and a finding counts only when its source ties the person to this race. Each is labelled by its source and linked to it. Candidates for soil and water, hospital and other small district boards and city clerks and treasurers show what they filed and, if they listed one, their campaign website. Never collected, for anyone: home or mailing addresses, phone numbers, e-mail, family, marital status, religion, health, ethnicity, income, employers, schools or legal troubles. No social media profile, people-search site, data broker or voter file is ever a source, and nobody was contacted.
web

Found on the open web. A birth year or an office held is labelled by the kind of page that states it: “according to” a government’s own page or the campaign, “as reported by” Wikipedia or a named news organization. An age from a birth year alone reads “about”, and offices found this way are listed, never added up into years of service. A blank means nothing was found, not that there is nothing.
own

Campaign websites. A candidate’s website is the address they filed with the list, or the campaign’s own site found on the open web and checked against the race it names; the race’s page says which. An address that no longer leads to the campaign is left out.
own
In their own words. The topics a campaign’s issues page lists are shown as headings, with a link to the page; nothing is summarized. Photos from a campaign’s own site are credited to it and linked.
page

The record, not a label. For a nonpartisan office a race’s page shows only what is on the record: a party’s own published endorsement, an earlier run or office under a party label, and the candidate’s own words on their own campaign site, each linked to where it stands. This site never calls a person or a place by a party of its own choosing.
results

How a place has voted. For a nonpartisan office the race’s page shows how the place voted in past partisan elections: the official precinct results, added up here by county, city or town and district on the lines in force at that election. It is not a prediction, it says nothing about any candidate or voter, and where very few people voted the split is left out.
polls

Polls of the statewide races are shown only from pollsters in the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative, who publish how each poll was done: the latest from up to five of them, each checked against the pollster’s own release, and our own average of the ten most recent, with the arithmetic shown. Polls by other pollsters are counted and named, not shown. A poll is a measure of opinion when it was taken, with a margin of error, not a forecast.
polls

Betting markets. Prices on Polymarket, a prediction market, are shown for the statewide races it lists, as information only: not a poll, not a forecast and not an official record. They are read from its public data, and prices move all day. Where Kalshi or PredictIt (two other markets) lists a race, the page says so and links to it, but shows none of its prices: their terms do not allow other sites to show them. A notice comes before any link to a market. The Civic Archive takes no money from any market and uses no referral links.
lists

The contests for Congress at the top of your ballot are the Congress pages’ own, from the state’s official candidate list: each name as printed, with its party label, in the ballot order the list gives (or by surname where it gives none), with its write-in and incumbent marks. Everything else about those candidates is on their race’s Congress page. Your U.S. House district is found from your precinct, where the map files place it, on your own device.
rules

Ballot questions. Each question’s official texts are shown word for word: the question as it will be printed and, where the record has them, the official summary, what a yes and a no vote do and the fiscal note, each labelled by who wrote it where the record says, and by its source. Where this site puts something in its own words (often the votes needed to pass and how the question got on the ballot), the question’s page says so beside it. Each side’s arguments in the official voter guide are linked, never reprinted.
page

Your ballot, printed or kept. “As it will look” draws your ballot as a printed sample ballot; it is a preview, not an official ballot, and your county’s own sample ballot is the authority. “Keep this ballot on my phone” saves the contests, the names, the questions’ words and the names of your districts and places in this device’s own storage, with the date, to open with no signal. No location, no address and no account: nothing is sent anywhere. “Forget my location and choices” removes it, and so does “Forget this ballot” on the kept page. Anyone holding your unlocked phone can see which districts a kept ballot is for.

changelog.title: Top movers, and breaking-news alerts for Election Night
items: Top movers: a ticker on the Forecasts page, on Election Night's Forecasts page and on the front page shows the races whose forecast moved most since the previous day's, like a stock ticker: the state, the office, the leading candidate's chance and how many points it moved, and "now leads" where the lead changed hands. Each one opens the race's chart. It stops when you point at it or move to it with the keyboard, has a Pause button, and never moves for anyone who has Motion off, Calm on or reduced motion on their device: the races then sit in a row you can scroll. Labelled Analysis.

Election Night alerts: on the night (from 4 p.m. Central on November 3), a banner across the top of every page brings the news as it comes: polls closing in each state, each state's first official results, a race whose live forecast passes 95%, a new leader in the live forecast, and projections. An early projection comes when the model gives a candidate 99% or more with at least a quarter of the expected vote counted; a full projection, in a stronger brass band, from half counted. Each says how much is counted, is labelled Analysis and "as reported, not final", and the official count decides. A projection that stops holding is withdrawn in an alert of its own. Pause, See all alerts and Close are there; nothing makes a sound; before the night the pages ask for nothing.

changelog.title: Forecasts stamped with the date and time, newest polls, ballots cast
items: Every forecast now carries the date and time it was made, so you can follow how it moved. The forecast record keeps a copy each morning until November 2, and another whenever a new run of the model changes anything, each listed by the date and time it was taken; each race's small line follows its chance from one copy to the next.

Each race's chart marks the model's earlier runs with their date and time, placed by the hour on the time line. On the Forecasts page each race says when its forecast was made, and from the standard level up a small line shows how the leading candidate's chance moved, run by run; the top of the page says when the newest run was made.

Newest polls: new polls by members of the Transparency Initiative, each checked against the pollster's own release, add 19 race results to the averages: CNN's polls by SSRS in Kansas, Maine, Michigan and Texas (Senate and governor), Emerson in Kansas, ActiVote in Texas, East Carolina University in South Carolina, Concord in South Dakota and Montana, and High Point University in North Carolina (Senate and Supreme Court). 16 results by other pollsters, in Alaska, Alabama, Iowa, Michigan, Montana, South Carolina and Texas, are shown apart and never averaged. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena polls of Minnesota and Florida, the Washington Post's of Kansas, Michigan State University's of Michigan) are listed as waiting, not shown. The poll finder no longer files a statewide poll under a House district.

Ballots cast so far: new counts from California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Maine, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas. South Dakota's newest weekly file is held back: one of its own totals does not match its party rows, so its page keeps the October 23 figures until the state corrects it.
The forecasts were made again with the new polls and counts.

changelog.title: Sandbox: Reading & access, in lanes
items: A second sandbox experiment, on the draft site only: the reading and access settings sorted into six lanes (Language, How much, Text, Colour and contrast, Motion and calm, Ready-made sets). Open a lane and its settings are tabs: click one to pin it open, as many as you like, and your pins are kept on this device. Open another lane and it opens to the left of the first, so several can be open at once; on a phone they line up in a strip you swipe through.
The Language lane comes first and names every language with a finished translation in its own words. Choosing one shows the page again in that language, with the lane still open.
The settings are the site's own, so whatever is chosen there carries to every page. Every other page still opens the usual panel.

changelog.title: Final-week polls, Texas specials, Connecticut's towns, Election Night readiness
items: Final-week polls: 32 more polls, each checked against the pollster's own release. Polls by members of the Transparency Initiative count in the averages: Marquette, Marist, Siena, Michigan State, Concord, Emerson, Targoz, ActiVote and the University of North Florida, across Senate and governor races in Wisconsin, Maine, New York, Michigan, Nebraska, Rhode Island, South Carolina and Florida, and U.S. House districts NY-17, WA-03 and KY-06. Polls by others are shown apart and never averaged; those paid for by a campaign or a party say so. Polls we could not check against their own release (the New York Times/Siena district polls, Emerson's subscriber-only district polls) are listed as waiting, not shown. The day's forecasts were made again with them.

Texas: the state's November 3 special elections for State House District 93 and State Senate District 22, the 276th District Court, a Democrat added to one judicial race, and nine declared write-ins are now on Texas's ballot pages, from the Secretary of State's own lists.

Connecticut: every town has now posted its sample ballot, and all are read: registrars of voters, town and school board contests, and every probate district now carry their candidates (110 local races, up from 76).

On state ballot pages, 43 kinds of local office that were listed at the end under their own titles (Florida's community development boards, library boards, receivers of taxes and others) now sit with the offices like them.

Election Night: Minnesota's saved results files are read about four times faster; Texas's two special elections and its judicial race are tied to the state's results; a new check holds back any state's file that shows votes before its polls close (three states' test files do today); and practice runs can no longer reach the public results.
Election Night counts 267 statewide races, and the U.S. page now names the District of Columbia's two offices apart from them. The Past results door now says all 50 states and DC are loaded.

State ballot pages: Georgia's and Virginia's mail-ballot notes no longer call October 23 "this Friday"; notes and source lines no longer describe how this site reads its files or show raw web addresses (each source's link is still there).

Wording: the news-outlet count now matches everywhere; the Method page says plainly that polls outside our average are shown apart; it says which Forecasts page lists every forecast; the privacy answers now name the Forecasts page's address look-up and street maps, and the Access page names the weather picture's one request; the page guide no longer says Minnesota is the only state with a forecast map.

changelog.title: A sandbox, and Anthropic's prospectus four ways
items: A sandbox on the draft site, for experiments: in no menu, not on the live site, and every page asks search engines not to list it.

Its first experiment is the prospectus Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, filed with the SEC on October 26, 2026, four ways. As filed: a link to the official copy on SEC.gov. In chapters: save the official copy from SEC.gov and open it in a reader that rebuilds it into its 27 chapters, with highlights, notes, search, a page-by-page view as filed, and a PDF of a chapter, the chapters you marked, your notes alone or the whole filing. The copy and your notes stay on your device; this site never holds the filing's text. In five minutes: about 1,230 words in the filing's own order, in our words, checked claim by claim against the filing. And an analysis of whether it reads as if an AI wrote it: whether text carries a mark that says so (it does not, for anyone to read), and the word counts studies tie to AI writing, beside eight other prospectuses, four of them filed before ChatGPT existed. Every figure there is labelled Analysis and says what it cannot tell you.
The pages say the site is built with the help of Claude, and that Anthropic had no part in them.

Ballots cast so far: California, South Dakota, Colorado, Louisiana, Oregon and South Carolina are current again, read from the new names and layouts their offices now use. Iowa's site now refuses programs and Washington shows its counts only inside a dashboard, so both wait for a hand-saved copy; Oklahoma has not posted yet. Building these pages takes under a second, down from half an hour.

changelog.title: Every state on the forecast map
items: Each state on both Forecasts pages now has its map and "Your ballot, as forecast", with Share: all 40 states with a forecast, not Minnesota alone. Use your location or type your address, and the page lists every race on your ballot there with the model's forecast where it has one. Your location stays on your device.
A state's map and its list of races load only when you open that state.
In the states that drew new congressional lines for 2026, the map says so, and your U.S. House district is found only from the new lines, never the old ones.

The nine states with new U.S. House districts for 2026 (Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas, Utah) now show those districts on the ballot maps, from the Census Bureau's 2026 plan files published October 6, and "Use my location" or a typed address finds your 2026 district there. Before, those maps showed only the state's outline.

A statewide board elected by district (Texas's State Board of Education and others) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is placed by its own district, or the page says it cannot tell which seat is yours.
Past results load from the site's own results store rather than from each copy of the site, which leaves more room for election week.

Where a state's precinct lines are not on file here, your ballot still lists its statewide races. A statewide board elected by district (a state board of education, a public service commission) is no longer put on every ballot in the state: it is counted among the races the page could not place, and the state's own ballot lookup is the authority.

s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission

State and Local Government, Chapter 3 Part A: Local Government, Louisiana House of Representatives

x.es: El concejo de la ciudad o del pueblo hace las leyes de la ciudad. También aprueba el presupuesto y fija los impuestos y las tarifas.

county_attorney.t: The county attorney brings criminal cases in county courts and is also the lawyer for county government. In some states this office is called the state's attorney.
s: Duties of Elected County Officials, Informational Bulletin No. 114, Kentucky Legislative Research Commission
Texas Constitution, Article 5 (Judicial Department), Texas Legislature

county_council.t: The county council makes the county's laws. A separate elected executive or mayor runs the county's departments.
s: Maryland at a Glance: Government (Charter counties), Maryland Manual, Maryland State Archives

x.es: El concejo del condado hace las leyes del condado. Un ejecutivo o un alcalde elegido por separado dirige los departamentos del condado.

county_treasurer.t: The county treasurer collects property taxes and keeps the county's money safe. The office shares it with schools, cities and other districts, but does not set how much is owed.

court_of_appeals.t: The court of appeals is the middle level of state courts. Its judges check trial court rulings for legal mistakes when one side appeals, and they do not hold new trials.

municipal_court.t: A municipal court is a city's own court. It handles broken city laws, traffic cases and minor crimes that happen in the city.
s: Courts of Limited Jurisdiction, Washington State Courts

x.es: Un tribunal municipal es el tribunal propio de una ciudad. Atiende las violaciones de las leyes de la ciudad, los casos de tránsito y los delitos menores que ocurren en la ciudad.

port_board.t: Port commissioners run a port district. Ports run public harbors and, in some places, airports, and they develop land for business and trade.
s: RCW 53.08, Port districts: powers, Washington State Legislature

x.es: Los comisionados portuarios dirigen un distrito portuario. Los distritos portuarios administran puertos públicos y, en algunos lugares, aeropuertos, y desarrollan terrenos para los negocios y el comercio.

sheriff.t: In most states the sheriff is the county's top law officer. The office keeps the peace, runs the jail and carries out court orders; in Kentucky it also collects property taxes.

x.es: En la mayoría de los estados, el alguacil es el principal agente de la ley del condado. La oficina mantiene la paz, dirige la cárcel y cumple las órdenes de los tribunales; en Kentucky, también cobra los impuestos sobre la propiedad.

state_house.t: The state House (called the Assembly or House of Delegates in some states) is the larger chamber. Its members write and vote on state laws and the state budget.

state_senate.t: The state Senate is the smaller of the Legislature's two chambers (Nebraska has only one). Senators write and vote on state laws and the state budget.

x.es: El Senado estatal es la más pequeña de las dos cámaras de la Legislatura (Nebraska tiene solo una). Los senadores redactan y votan las leyes estatales y el presupuesto del estado.

utility_board.t: These boards run a public utility, such as a power, water or city utility. They oversee the service and set its rates.
